questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a measure that helps reduce the spread of HIV?
questions.x: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, so they do not prevent HIV. Blood screening, sterile syringes and safe sexual behaviour all block known routes of spread.

questions.q: Most plant viruses contain RNA. An exception that has double-stranded DNA is:
questions.x: Cauliflower mosaic virus is a well-known plant virus with double-stranded DNA. Tobacco mosaic virus and potato virus X are RNA viruses, and cotton leaf curl virus has single-stranded DNA.

questions.q: Before stored glycogen in liver and muscle can be used in respiration, it is broken down into:
questions.x: Glycogen is a polymer of glucose. It is broken down to glucose (as glucose phosphate), which then enters glycolysis.

questions.q: During prolonged fasting, the liver makes new glucose from the carbon skeletons of some amino acids. This process is called:
questions.x: Gluconeogenesis means formation of new glucose from non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids and glycerol. Glycogenesis is the making of glycogen from glucose.

questions.q: Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), the hormone detected in pregnancy tests, is chemically a:
questions.x: hCG, like FSH and LH, is a glycoprotein hormone: a protein with carbohydrate chains. Steroid hormones are lipids.

questions.q: A lipoprotein is a conjugated molecule made of:
questions.x: A lipoprotein combines lipid with protein. Lipid plus carbohydrate is a glycolipid, and protein plus carbohydrate is a glycoprotein.

questions.q: The mucus lining the stomach, rich in glycoproteins, helps to:
o: Absorb most of the glucose from food
Protect the stomach wall from acid and pepsin
questions.x: The glycoprotein mucus forms a protective barrier so that the stomach's own acid and pepsin do not digest its wall.

questions.q: A membrane molecule, on hydrolysis, yields fatty acids, a sugar and an alcohol, but no amino acids and no phosphate. The molecule is a:
questions.x: Fatty acids and an alcohol show a lipid, and the sugar shows a carbohydrate part, so it is a glycolipid. Glycoproteins and lipoproteins would give amino acids, and a phospholipid would give phosphate.

questions.q: A transplanted kidney may be rejected because the recipient's immune cells recognise foreign markers on the donor's cells. These markers are mainly:
questions.x: Surface glycoproteins act as 'self' antigens; immune cells recognise a donor's different glycoproteins as foreign. Molecules inside the cell are not exposed to them.

questions.q: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACCGGAAAACT-5′. How many amino acids will the polypeptide made from it contain?
questions.x: The mRNA is 5′-AUG GCC UUU UGA-3′. AUG, GCC and UUU code for three amino acids, and UGA is a stop codon, which codes for none.

questions.q: Fat stored in a camel's hump helps it survive in the desert because oxidation of fat releases energy and:
o: Salts that hold water in the body
A large amount of metabolic water
questions.x: Oxidation of fat produces carbon dioxide and a large quantity of water (metabolic water), which helps desert animals. It uses oxygen rather than releasing it.

questions.q: Which group of vitamins dissolves in fats rather than in water?
o: The B-group vitamins and vitamin C
Vitamins A, D, E and K
Vitamin C and vitamin D only
questions.x: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and are absorbed and stored along with lipids. The B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble.

questions.q: During translation, a ribosome moves along the mRNA, reading its codons in the direction:
o: From both ends towards the middle
From the middle towards both ends
questions.x: Translation starts near the 5′ end at the start codon and proceeds codon by codon towards the 3′ end.

questions.q: Phospholipids placed in water arrange themselves into a double layer mainly because:
o: Their hydrophobic tails are kept away from water while their hydrophilic heads face the water
Their tails dissolve in water while their heads avoid it
Water forms covalent bonds with their fatty acid tails
They react with water and are hydrolysed into a bilayer
questions.x: Water's polarity attracts the charged phosphate heads but excludes the non-polar tails. The tails therefore turn inwards, away from water, forming a bilayer.

questions.q: When fructose forms a ring, the ring contains:
o: Five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom
Four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom
Six carbon atoms and no oxygen atom
Three carbon atoms and two oxygen atoms
questions.x: Fructose forms a five-membered (furanose) ring of four carbons and one oxygen. Glucose forms a six-membered (pyranose) ring of five carbons and one oxygen.

questions.q: Enzymes are vital to living cells because they:
o: Supply the energy that reactions need
Speed up chemical reactions without being used up
Raise the temperature of the cell
Are used up in every reaction they catalyse
questions.x: Enzymes are catalysts: they lower the energy needed to start a reaction and can be used again and again. They do not supply energy or heat the cell.

questions.q: The fixed position that a gene occupies on a chromosome is called its:
questions.x: A gene's locus is its specific place on a chromosome. Alleles are alternative forms of a gene found at the same locus.

questions.q: The term 'eukaryotic' comes from Greek roots describing a cell with a:
questions.x: Eu means true and karyon means nucleus, so eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus surrounded by a nuclear envelope.

questions.q: Each skeletal muscle fibre contains many nuclei. Such a cell is described as:
questions.x: A skeletal muscle fibre forms by fusion of many cells, so it has many nuclei and is multinucleate. Enucleate means having no nucleus, as in mature red blood cells.

questions.q: The nucleus was discovered in plant cells in 1831 by:
questions.x: Robert Brown described the nucleus in orchid cells in 1831. Robert Hooke named the cell in 1665, and Golgi described the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: The refractory period of a neuron sets an upper limit on the:
o: Number of impulses it can carry each second
questions.x: A new action potential cannot start until the refractory period ends, so only a limited number of impulses can pass each second.

questions.q: The pupil reflex to bright light differs from the knee-jerk reflex in that the pupil reflex is:
o: Spinal and monosynaptic, while the knee jerk is cranial and polysynaptic
Conditioned, while the knee jerk is unconditioned
Cranial and polysynaptic, while the knee jerk is spinal and monosynaptic
Cranial and monosynaptic, while the knee jerk is spinal and polysynaptic
questions.x: The pupil reflex is integrated in the midbrain and passes through several neurons, so it is cranial and polysynaptic. The knee jerk is a spinal stretch reflex with one synapse. Both are unconditioned.

questions.q: The midbrain acts mainly as a:
o: Relay and reflex centre for visual and auditory impulses
Centre for controlling heartbeat and breathing
questions.x: The midbrain relays visual and auditory information and coordinates reflexes such as the pupil reflex. Heartbeat and breathing are medulla functions, and intelligence belongs to the cerebrum.

questions.q: A spinal nerve supplying part of the leg is cut beyond the point where its dorsal and ventral roots join. In the area it supplies:
o: Only sensation is lost, while reflexes remain
Only voluntary movement is lost, while sensation remains
Sensation remains, but reflexes are lost
Sensation, reflexes and voluntary movement are all lost
questions.x: Beyond the junction of the roots the spinal nerve is mixed, carrying both sensory and motor fibres. Cutting it stops impulses in both directions, so sensation, reflexes and voluntary movement are all lost.

questions.q: The association areas of the cerebral cortex function to:
o: Interpret sensory information and link it with memory and motor responses
Directly control the rate of heartbeat
Relay impulses from the spinal cord to the cerebellum
questions.x: Association areas analyse and combine information from the sensory areas, relate it to past experience and help plan responses. Heart rate is controlled by the medulla.

questions.q: A person touches a hot iron and feels a sharp burning pain. The pain is first detected by:
o: Pacinian corpuscles deep in the dermis
Meissner's corpuscles in the dermal papillae
Nociceptors, which are free nerve endings
questions.x: Pain arising from damaging heat is detected by nociceptors, which are free nerve endings. Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles detect touch and pressure; baroreceptors lie in artery walls.

questions.q: Hair cells in the semicircular canals of the inner ear are stimulated by:
o: Changes in the temperature of the blood
questions.x: The semicircular canals detect rotation of the head for balance; their hair cells are mechanoreceptors moved by the fluid inside. Sound is detected in the cochlea.

questions.q: Conditioned reflexes are established mainly through:
o: Repeated pairing of a new stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus
The growth of new spinal nerves
A single exposure to a stimulus without any reinforcement
questions.x: A conditioned reflex forms when a neutral stimulus is repeatedly given together with an unconditioned stimulus, as with the bell and food. It is acquired, not inherited, and needs repetition.

questions.q: An enzyme reaction has plenty of enzyme but very little substrate. Which change would increase the rate the most?
o: Moving the pH away from the optimum
questions.x: With few substrate molecules, most active sites are empty, so extra enzyme helps little. Extra substrate fills more active sites and raises the rate.

questions.q: An enzyme's rate was measured at substrate concentrations of 1, 2, 4 and 8 mM, giving 10, 20, 35 and 36 units. Between 4 and 8 mM, the rate is limited mainly by:
o: A temperature that is too high
A pH that is too low
questions.x: Doubling substrate from 4 to 8 mM barely changes the rate, so the active sites are nearly all occupied; the amount of enzyme now limits the rate.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a cofactor?
questions.x: The apoenzyme is the protein part of the enzyme itself. Coenzymes, prosthetic groups and metal ions are the non-protein cofactors it may need.

questions.q: Egg white turns solid and white when boiled. The change in an enzyme that is similar to this is:
o: Denaturation of its protein by heat
questions.x: Egg white is mostly protein; heat breaks the weak bonds holding its shape, just as heat denatures an enzyme. The amino acid chain itself is not hydrolysed.

questions.q: Most enzyme names end in '-ase'. Which of the following enzymes is an exception to this naming rule?
questions.x: Pepsin, like trypsin and rennin, kept an older name that does not end in '-ase'. Lipase, maltase and sucrase follow the usual rule.

questions.q: The gases of the Earth's primitive atmosphere are thought to have come mainly from:
o: Volcanic eruptions releasing gases from the Earth's interior
questions.x: Early atmospheric gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia and hydrogen were released by volcanic outgassing. Photosynthesis came much later and added oxygen.

questions.q: Why can a mutation that occurs in a person's skin cell NOT be passed on to his children?
o: Mutations are always repaired before birth
Skin cells are body cells and do not form gametes
Skin cells contain only half the chromosomes
questions.x: Only changes in germ cells reach the offspring. A skin cell is a somatic cell, so its mutation stays in that person's body.

questions.q: A fair-skinned family moves to a very sunny region and their skin becomes darker. According to Lamarck, children born to them afterwards would:
o: Be born with darker skin than their parents had at birth
Be born with the original fair skin
Have darker skin only if a mutation occurred
questions.x: Lamarck believed acquired changes such as a tan are inherited. In reality a tan is a change in body cells, so the children are born with the family's inherited skin colour.

questions.q: HIV is classified as a retrovirus because it:
o: Has DNA and makes RNA from it
Has no nucleic acid at all
Has RNA and makes DNA from it by reverse transcriptase
questions.x: Retroviruses carry RNA and use reverse transcriptase to copy it into DNA, the reverse of the usual DNA-to-RNA flow.

questions.q: Strong contractions of the uterus during childbirth are stimulated by:
questions.x: Oxytocin, released from the posterior pituitary, causes the myometrium to contract during labour. Progesterone does the opposite during pregnancy and keeps the uterus quiet.

questions.q: Semen is slightly alkaline. This helps the sperm mainly because it:
o: Supplies fructose as an energy source
Keeps the sperm still until ejaculation
Neutralises the acidity of the vagina
questions.x: The vagina is acidic, which harms sperm; the alkaline secretions in semen neutralise this acid. Fructose for energy comes from the seminal vesicles, but that is a separate function from alkalinity.

questions.q: If all the parathyroid glands were removed, the most direct effect on calcium would be:
o: A fall in blood calcium, because less calcium is released from bone
A rise in blood calcium, because bone is dissolved faster
Faster growth of the epiphyseal plates
Softening of all the body's cartilage
questions.x: Parathormone normally stimulates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone. Without it, less calcium leaves the bone and blood calcium falls.

questions.q: In a newborn baby, the soft spots (fontanelles) between the skull bones are:
o: Synovial joints that remain freely movable for life
Cartilaginous discs like those between vertebrae
Membrane-covered gaps that later close into immovable sutures
Gliding joints that allow the bones to slide freely
questions.x: Fontanelles are areas of fibrous membrane between the growing skull bones. As the bones grow they close, and the bones are then joined by fibrous, immovable sutures.

questions.q: Which pairing of a supporting tissue with a component of its matrix is correct?
o: Hyaline cartilage – thick bundles of yellow elastic fibres
Fibrocartilage – no fibres of any kind
Bone – collagen fibres and calcium phosphate
questions.x: Bone matrix combines collagen fibres with calcium phosphate. Elastic fibres are typical of elastic cartilage, fibrocartilage is rich in collagen bundles, and cartilage is not normally calcified.

questions.q: In a young child, red bone marrow is found in:
o: Nearly all bones, including the shafts of long bones
Only the flat bones such as the ribs and sternum
Only the ends of the femur
questions.x: In young children almost every bone, including long-bone shafts, holds red marrow. Later the shafts fill with yellow marrow and red marrow becomes limited mainly to flat bones and the ends of long bones.

questions.q: A student lists features of freely movable joints. Which item on the list is NOT correct?
o: They have a cavity containing synovial fluid
Their bone ends are covered with articular cartilage
They are enclosed by a joint capsule
They join the flat bones of the adult skull
questions.x: The flat bones of the adult skull are joined by fibrous sutures, not synovial joints. A cavity with fluid, articular cartilage and a capsule are all features of synovial joints.

questions.q: Elastic cartilage, rich in yellow elastic fibres, is found in the wall of the:
questions.x: Elastic cartilage supports the pinna, the epiglottis and the Eustachian tube. The trachea has hyaline cartilage, while intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis contain fibrocartilage.

questions.q: The sinoatrial (SA) node, the pacemaker of the heart, is made of:
o: Nerve cells of the vagus nerve
questions.x: The SA node is a patch of modified cardiac muscle that starts each heartbeat on its own. Nerves such as the vagus only change the rate.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle cells contain very many mitochondria. This suits them because they:
o: Contract continuously and depend on aerobic respiration
Respire mainly anaerobically to make lactic acid
questions.x: The heart beats throughout life without rest, so its cells need a steady supply of ATP from aerobic respiration in mitochondria.

questions.q: Two sons are born to an XᴴXʰ mother and an XᴴY father. The chance that only one of the two boys is hemophilic is:
questions.x: Each son has a 1/2 chance of being affected. Exactly one affected can happen two ways (first or second son): 2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/2.

questions.q: An individual of genotype AaBbCC forms gametes, with the genes assorting independently. Which statement is correct?
o: Half of the gametes carry the c allele
It forms eight types of gametes
No gamete carries the A allele together with the b allele
Every gamete carries the C allele
questions.x: The individual is homozygous CC, so every gamete gets C. Only the two heterozygous genes vary, giving 2 × 2 = 4 gamete types, and the combination of A with b is one of them.

questions.q: Crossing over between genes A and B produces new allele combinations only when the individual is:
questions.x: If either locus is homozygous, exchanging segments swaps identical alleles and nothing new forms. Both loci must be heterozygous for recombinants to arise.

questions.q: In birds, the sex of a chick is decided by:
o: The type of sperm produced by the father
The temperature at which the egg is kept
The number of autosomes in the egg
The type of egg produced by the mother
questions.x: The hen (ZW) makes Z-bearing and W-bearing eggs, while the cock (ZZ) makes only Z sperm. So the egg decides the sex, unlike in humans.

questions.q: Why are recombinant offspring of linked genes fewer than the parental types?
o: A crossover between the two genes occurs in only some meiotic cells
Crossing over occurs only in males
questions.x: In most meiotic cells no crossover happens between the two loci, and even a crossover affects only two of the four chromatids. So parental gametes stay in the majority.

questions.q: In a monohybrid cross showing incomplete dominance, the F2 phenotypic ratio and genotypic ratio are:
o: Both 1 : 2 : 1, because each genotype has its own phenotype
questions.x: With incomplete dominance the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, so each of the three genotypes looks different and both ratios are 1 : 2 : 1. Under complete dominance the phenotypic ratio would be 3 : 1.

questions.q: Two heterozygous pea plants (Rr × Rr) produce 600 seeds. About how many seeds are expected to be heterozygous (Rr)?
questions.x: Rr × Rr gives 1/4 RR, 1/2 Rr and 1/4 rr. Half of 600 is 300. 450 would be the number of round seeds (3/4), not heterozygous ones.

questions.q: In hemophilia, the part of blood that is deficient is:
o: A clotting factor protein in plasma
questions.x: Hemophilia is a lack of a plasma clotting factor, such as factor VIII. Platelets, red cells and white cells are normal.

questions.q: Compared with veins, lymph vessels have:
o: Muscular walls that beat like a heart
questions.x: Lymph vessels resemble veins but are thinner walled and have even more valves. They have no pump of their own.

questions.q: Tissue fluid that bathes the body's cells differs from blood plasma mainly in having:
questions.x: Tissue fluid is plasma that has leaked out of capillaries without the large proteins and cells. Its small solutes, like glucose, are at similar levels.

questions.q: Tissue fluid enters lymph capillaries easily because their walls:
o: Have overlapping endothelial cells that act as one-way flaps
Contain pumps that pull fluid in
Are lined with red blood cells
questions.x: The endothelial cells of lymph capillaries overlap loosely, opening inward to let fluid in but closing to stop it leaking out.

questions.q: Most plasma proteins stay inside the blood capillaries because they:
o: Are actively pumped back by the endothelium
Are destroyed as soon as they leave
Are too large to pass through the capillary walls
Are bound to the red blood cells
questions.x: Plasma proteins are large molecules that cannot easily cross the capillary wall, so they remain in the blood and create its osmotic pressure.

questions.q: A pulse can be felt in arteries but not in veins because:
o: The pressure surges are smoothed out before blood reaches the veins
Veins carry no blood between heartbeats
Veins have stiffer walls than arteries
Blood flows away from the heart in veins
questions.x: Pressure waves from each ventricular contraction are damped in the arterioles and capillaries, so blood in veins flows steadily at low pressure.

questions.q: AIDS is an example of:
questions.x: AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) is caused by HIV, which weakens the immune system during life. It is not inherited, and the body is not attacking itself.

questions.q: If blood group A is transfused into a person of blood group B, the donor red cells clump because the recipient's plasma contains:
questions.x: A group B person carries anti-A antibodies in plasma. These bind the A antigens on the donated cells and agglutinate them.

questions.q: When the lungs are well inflated, stretch receptors in the walls of the bronchioles send impulses to the brain that:
o: Start a cough to clear the airways
Increase the rate and depth of inspiration
Stop inspiration so that the lungs are not over-inflated
Close the epiglottis over the glottis
questions.x: Stretch receptors send impulses along the vagus nerve to the respiratory centre, which switches off inspiration and lets expiration begin (the Hering–Breuer reflex). This protects the lungs from over-stretching.

questions.q: A smoker who stops suddenly feels irritable, restless and craves a cigarette for some days. This is because:
o: Carbon monoxide levels in the blood have risen
Tar is being released from the lungs into the brain
The body has become dependent on nicotine
questions.x: Nicotine is addictive; when it is withdrawn the dependent smoker has withdrawal symptoms such as craving and irritability. Carbon monoxide levels actually fall after stopping.

questions.q: 100 mL of fully oxygenated arterial blood carries a total of about:
questions.x: Because of haemoglobin, 100 mL of arterial blood carries about 20 mL of oxygen. Only about 0.3 mL of this is dissolved in the plasma; the rest is bound as oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.q: Goblet cells in the lining of the respiratory tract secrete:
questions.x: Goblet cells are single-celled glands in the ciliated lining of the airways; they secrete sticky mucus that traps dust and microbes. Surfactant is made by cells in the alveolar wall, not by goblet cells.

questions.q: The root of a tooth is covered by a thin, bone-like layer that helps fix the tooth in its socket. This layer is the:
questions.x: Cementum covers the root and, with the fibres of the periodontal ligament, holds the tooth in the jaw socket. Enamel covers only the crown, and dentine lies beneath both.

questions.q: Which statement about bile is correct?
o: It contains lipase that digests fats
It is acidic and helps pepsin to work
It is made and stored by the pancreas
It contains bile salts but no digestive enzymes
questions.x: Bile contains no enzymes; its bile salts emulsify fats, and its alkalinity helps neutralise acid chyme. It is made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

questions.q: Besides ammonia, which nitrogenous compound is excreted by many marine bony fishes?
questions.x: Trimethylamine oxide is a nitrogen-containing waste of marine bony fishes. Glycogen, lactic acid and carbon dioxide contain no nitrogen.

questions.q: During a dry season in mud, the African lungfish switches from excreting ammonia to making urea. Urea is useful here because it:
o: Is a gas that escapes easily through the skin
Needs more water to excrete than ammonia
Is completely insoluble and forms crystals
Is far less toxic and can be held in the body until water returns
questions.x: Without water to flush ammonia away, the fish makes urea, which is much less toxic and can safely accumulate until it can be excreted.

questions.q: Which pair of substances both pass freely from the glomerulus into the filtrate?
questions.x: Small molecules such as glucose and urea are filtered freely. Albumin and fibrinogen are plasma proteins and red cells are far too large, so each of the other pairs contains something that is held back.

questions.q: The concave inner border of each bean-shaped kidney, where the hilum lies, faces:
o: Towards the front wall of the abdomen
Outwards, towards the side of the body
questions.x: The kidneys lie on either side of the backbone with their concave borders facing inwards towards it. Renal vessels and the ureter enter or leave at the hilum on this side.

questions.q: 'Goose bumps' appear on human skin in the cold because:
o: Tiny muscles attached to the hair follicles contract
Fat cells under the skin divide
questions.x: Contraction of the hair erector muscles pulls the hairs upright and raises small bumps; in humans this gives little insulation.

questions.q: Whales and seals living in icy water keep warm mainly because they have:
o: A thick layer of fat (blubber) under the skin that insulates the body
A large surface area to volume ratio
questions.x: Blubber is a poor conductor of heat, so it greatly reduces heat loss to the cold water. A large surface area to volume ratio would increase heat loss.

questions.q: The vasa recta are found mainly in the:
questions.x: The vasa recta are long, straight capillary loops that run down into the medulla beside the loops of Henle and back up again.

questions.q: Which pair of animals are both uricotelic?
questions.x: Birds and insects excrete uric acid. Cows, adult frogs, humans and sharks are ureotelic; goldfish and tadpoles are ammonotelic.

questions.q: A person with diabetes insipidus (no ADH) may pass many litres of urine a day, yet far less than the 180 litres of filtrate formed. Why?
o: Most water is reabsorbed in the PCT and loop of Henle whether or not ADH is present
The glomeruli stop filtering when ADH is absent
The bladder reabsorbs most of the water
questions.x: ADH controls only the final, facultative water uptake in the DCT and collecting duct. The large obligatory reabsorption in the PCT and loop continues, so most of the filtrate is still reclaimed.

questions.q: Genetically modified goats and sheep have been used to produce human proteins for treatment, such as clotting proteins, by:
o: Releasing the protein in their urine as a hormone
Secreting the human protein in their milk
Storing the protein in their wool
Producing it in their red blood cells
questions.x: The human gene is joined to a promoter that is active only in the mammary gland, so the protein is secreted into the milk, from which it is collected and purified. This is sometimes called pharming.

questions.q: In a paternity test using DNA profiles, every band in the child's profile should be present in:
o: Both the mother's and the father's profiles
Either the mother's profile or the true father's profile
questions.x: A child inherits half its DNA from each parent, so each band comes from one parent or the other. Bands not found in the mother must match the true father.

questions.q: An mRNA vaccine, such as some COVID-19 vaccines, protects against the virus by:
o: Inserting the whole viral genome into human chromosomes
Delivering ready-made antibodies against the virus
Supplying mRNA that body cells use to make a viral protein, which the immune system then responds to
Containing live weakened virus that multiplies in the body
questions.x: The mRNA is translated by the person's own cells into the viral spike protein, which acts as an antigen and triggers antibodies and memory cells. The mRNA does not enter the chromosomes, and no live virus is given.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a technique with its use?
o: PCR: separating DNA fragments by size
Gel electrophoresis: making millions of copies of DNA
ELISA: detecting an antigen or antibody in a blood sample
DNA ligase: detecting a gene in a sample
questions.x: ELISA uses enzyme-linked antibodies to detect antigens or antibodies. PCR amplifies DNA, gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size, and ligase joins DNA pieces.

questions.q: Ethane burns according to 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. How many moles of O₂ are needed to burn 1 mol of ethane completely?
questions.x: The ratio O₂ : C₂H₆ is 7 : 2, so 1 mol of ethane needs 7/2 = 3.5 mol O₂. Using 7 mol forgets that the equation shows 2 mol of ethane.

questions.q: For C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O, 1 mol of propane is burnt in 4 mol of oxygen. What is the maximum amount of CO₂ formed?
questions.x: 1 mol propane needs 5 mol O₂, so O₂ (4 mol) is limiting. CO₂ = 4 × 3/5 = 2.4 mol. 3 mol assumes all the propane burns.

questions.q: Which ion has the configuration [Ar] 3d⁵? (Cr = 24, Mn = 25, Fe = 26, Co = 27)
questions.x: Mn is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²; losing the two 4s electrons gives Mn²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵. Cr²⁺ is 3d⁴, Fe²⁺ 3d⁶ and Co²⁺ 3d⁷.

questions.q: Which species does NOT have the same electronic configuration as argon (Z = 18)?
questions.x: K⁺, Ca²⁺ and S²⁻ each have 18 electrons, like argon. Na⁺ has 10 electrons, the configuration of neon.

questions.q: The energy of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is −1312 kJ mol⁻¹. The ionisation energy of hydrogen is therefore:
questions.x: Ionisation takes the electron from n = 1 (−1312 kJ mol⁻¹) to infinity (0), so 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ must be supplied; ionisation energy is positive.

questions.q: An ideal gas could never be liquefied, however much it was cooled or compressed, because:
o: Its molecules occupy the whole container volume
Its molecules have no attractive forces between them
questions.x: Liquefaction needs attractive forces to hold molecules together. The ideal gas model assumes none, so only real gases, which do attract, can be liquefied.

questions.q: What is the density of oxygen gas, O₂, at 2 atm and 273 K? (O = 16; 0.0821 × 273 ≈ 22.4)
questions.x: d = PM/RT = (2 × 32)/22.4 ≈ 2.86 g dm⁻³. Forgetting the pressure of 2 atm gives 1.43, the density at STP.

questions.q: Which pair gives two values of R that are BOTH correct?
o: 8.314 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 0.0821 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 1.987 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
62.4 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
questions.x: R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The value 1.987 is in calories, and 62.4 is in dm³ mm Hg.

questions.q: As most liquids are warmed, their density:
o: Decreases, because the volume increases while the mass stays the same
Increases, because the molecules move faster
Stays the same, because the mass does not change
questions.x: Density = mass/volume. Warming makes most liquids expand, so the same mass occupies more volume and density falls. Water between 0 and 4 °C is the exception.

questions.q: The ionic radii are Mg²⁺ 72 pm and O²⁻ 140 pm. Using radius-ratio rules, the coordination number of Mg²⁺ in MgO is:
questions.x: Radius ratio = 72/140 ≈ 0.51, which lies between 0.414 and 0.732, giving octahedral coordination of 6, as in the rock-salt structure.

questions.q: An atom located at the midpoint of an edge of a cubic unit cell contributes what fraction of itself to that unit cell?
questions.x: An edge is shared by 4 unit cells, so each cell gets 1/4 of the atom. A face atom contributes 1/2 and a corner atom 1/8.

questions.q: Adding which substance to a solution of ethanoic acid would NOT suppress its ionisation?
questions.x: NaCl supplies neither H⁺ nor CH₃COO⁻, so it has no common ion with ethanoic acid. The other three each supply one of these ions.

questions.q: At the same temperature and pressure, 30 dm³ of hydrogen reacts completely with excess nitrogen. The volume of ammonia formed is:
questions.x: 3 volumes of H₂ give 2 volumes of NH₃, so 30 dm³ H₂ gives 30 × 2/3 = 20 dm³ NH₃.

questions.q: C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g) has ΔH positive. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of H₂?
questions.x: The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating favours it. Higher pressure favours the left (1 gas mol against 2), removing steam shifts it left, and a catalyst has no effect on yield.

questions.q: A mixture of petrol vapour and air does not burn until a spark is passed through it. The spark:
o: Acts as a catalyst that is used up
Changes the enthalpy change of combustion
Supplies the activation energy needed to start the reaction
questions.x: Combustion is exothermic, but the molecules first need energy to reach the activated complex. The spark provides this; the heat released then keeps the reaction going.

questions.q: For a reversible reaction, the forward activation energy is 120 kJ mol⁻¹ and the reverse activation energy is 80 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH of the forward reaction is:
questions.x: ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse) = 120 − 80 = +40 kJ mol⁻¹. The forward reaction climbs higher than the reverse, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: A catalyst is a substance that:
o: Is used up completely during the reaction
Increases the yield of products at equilibrium
Changes the rate of a reaction but is chemically unchanged at the end
Always raises the temperature of the reaction mixture
questions.x: A catalyst alters the rate and is recovered chemically unchanged. It does not change the equilibrium yield.

questions.q: Standard enthalpies of combustion of substances are always:
o: Positive, because oxygen bonds must be broken
Positive for elements and negative for compounds
Negative, because combustion gives out heat
questions.x: Combustion is always exothermic, so ΔH of combustion is negative for every fuel.

questions.q: The internal energy of a system falls by 80 J while the system does 30 J of work on the surroundings. What is q? (ΔE = q + w)
questions.x: ΔE = −80 J and w = −30 J (work done by the system). q = ΔE − w = −80 − (−30) = −50 J, so the system gives out 50 J of heat.

questions.q: In a working Daniell cell (Zn in ZnSO₄, Cu in CuSO₄), which electrode loses mass?
questions.x: Zinc is oxidised at the anode (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and dissolves, while copper is deposited on the copper cathode, which gains mass.

questions.q: In 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O, which statement is correct?
o: Carbon is reduced from +4 to +3 and each Mn loses 5 electrons
Carbon is oxidised from +3 to +4 and each Mn gains 3 electrons
Carbon is oxidised from +3 to +4 and each Mn gains 5 electrons
questions.x: C in C₂O₄²⁻: 2x − 8 = −2, x = +3; in CO₂ it is +4. Mn falls from +7 to +2 (5 electrons each); 2 × 5 = 10 matches 10 C × 1.

questions.q: Which molecule has polar bonds but is non-polar overall?
questions.x: SiF₄ is tetrahedral with four identical Si–F dipoles that cancel. NF₃ is pyramidal and OF₂ is bent, so they are polar; HF has only one polar bond.

questions.q: What is the shape of oxygen difluoride, OF₂, in which oxygen carries two lone pairs besides its two O–F bonds?
questions.x: Four electron pairs are arranged roughly tetrahedrally, but only two are bonds, so the molecule is bent like water.

questions.q: The basic idea of VSEPR theory is that the electron pairs in the valence shell of a central atom:
o: Attract one another and crowd together on one side
Are all shared equally with the surrounding atoms
Move into the inner shells of the central atom
Repel one another and stay as far apart as possible
questions.x: Bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom repel each other, so they take up positions as far apart as possible. That arrangement decides the shape of the molecule.

questions.q: Which of these Group IV elements is a typical metal?
questions.x: Metallic character increases down Group IV: carbon is a non-metal, silicon and germanium are metalloids, and tin and lead are metals.

questions.q: Which Group II chloride has the most ionic character?
questions.x: Ba²⁺ is the largest Group II ion with the lowest polarising power, so BaCl₂ is the most ionic; BeCl₂ is largely covalent.

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons does a gaseous Co²⁺ ion have (Co, Z = 27)?
questions.x: Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²; losing the two 4s electrons gives Co²⁺ = 3d⁷. Five electrons go singly into the five 3d orbitals and two more pair up, leaving 3 unpaired. Seven is the total d count, not the unpaired count.

questions.q: The heteroatom in the ring of furan, C₄H₄O, is:
questions.x: Furan has a five-membered ring of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom. Pyrrole contains nitrogen and thiophene sulphur.

questions.q: In propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃, the hybridisation of the carbons from the CH₂ end to the CH₃ end is:
questions.x: Both carbons of the double bond are sp², while the CH₃ carbon has four single bonds and is sp³.

questions.q: Pent-1-ene is one of several non-cyclic alkenes with five carbons and ten hydrogens. Ignoring cis–trans forms, the total number of such alkenes is:
questions.x: They are pent-1-ene, pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-1-ene, 3-methylbut-1-ene and 2-methylbut-2-ene: five structural isomers.

questions.q: The double-headed arrow (↔) written between the two Kekulé structures of benzene shows that:
o: The two structures are in a rapid chemical equilibrium
One structure is converted completely into the other
They are contributing structures of one hybrid, not two substances in equilibrium
The molecule vibrates between two shapes
questions.x: ↔ means resonance: the real molecule is one structure intermediate between those drawn. An equilibrium between two real substances is shown by ⇌.

questions.q: The name 2-ethylpropane is wrong. The structure it describes is correctly named:
questions.x: 2-ethylpropane is CH₃CH(C₂H₅)CH₃, whose longest chain is four carbons with a methyl on carbon 2: 2-methylbutane. An ethyl group on carbon 2 always means a longer chain was missed.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a termination step in the chlorination of methane?
questions.x: Termination removes radicals by joining two of them. CH₃• + Cl₂ produces a new radical, Cl•, so it is a propagation step.

questions.q: Ethyne reacts with one mole of hydrogen chloride. The product, used to make PVC, is:
questions.x: One HCl adds across the triple bond to give CH₂=CHCl, chloroethene, whose polymer is polyvinyl chloride.

questions.q: When ethyne loses H⁺ from one carbon, the anion HC≡C⁻ that is formed is called the:
questions.x: Salts of this anion, such as sodium acetylide, are called acetylides. Ethoxide is C₂H₅O⁻, from ethanol.

questions.q: Isopropyl chloride is the common name of the alkyl halide whose IUPAC name is:
questions.x: The isopropyl group is (CH₃)₂CH–, so isopropyl chloride is (CH₃)₂CHCl, 2-chloropropane. 1-Chloropropane is n-propyl chloride.

questions.q: Elimination of one molecule of HCl from C₄H₉Cl gives an organic product with the molecular formula:
questions.x: Removing H and Cl from C₄H₉Cl leaves C₄H₈, a butene. C₄H₉OH would be the substitution product.

questions.q: Benzyl alcohol, C₆H₅CH₂OH, contains a benzene ring and an –OH group, yet it is classed as an alcohol and not a phenol because:
o: Its –OH group is attached directly to the ring
It is more acidic than phenol
The –OH is on an sp³ carbon of the side chain, not directly on the ring
questions.x: A phenol has –OH bonded directly to an aromatic ring carbon. In benzyl alcohol the –OH is on the CH₂ carbon, so it behaves as a primary alcohol and is less acidic than phenol.

questions.q: Structurally, an alcohol can be regarded as a derivative of water in which:
o: Both hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl groups
The oxygen atom is replaced by a carbon atom
One hydrogen atom is replaced by a phenyl ring
One hydrogen atom is replaced by an alkyl group
questions.x: Replacing one H of H–O–H by an alkyl group gives R–O–H, an alcohol. Replacing both gives an ether, R–O–R′; replacing one by a benzene ring gives a phenol.

questions.q: When an aldehyde is warmed with Fehling's solution, a positive result is a colour change from:
o: Deep blue to a brick-red precipitate
questions.x: Fehling's solution is deep blue because of Cu²⁺; the aldehyde reduces this to Cu₂O, a brick-red precipitate. Orange to green is the change for acidified dichromate.

questions.q: Which reagent would NOT convert butanone into butan-2-ol?
o: LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then dilute acid
questions.x: Butanone → butan-2-ol is a reduction. NaBH₄, LiAlH₄ and H₂/Ni are reducing agents; acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ is an oxidising agent, so it cannot do this.

questions.q: Methylbenzene (toluene) is heated with alkaline KMnO₄ and then acidified. The organic product is:
questions.x: Strong oxidation converts the side-chain –CH₃ on a benzene ring into –COOH, giving C₆H₅COOH.

questions.q: A substance that resembles the substrate and occupies an enzyme's active site, slowing the reaction, is called a:
questions.x: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site. Coenzymes and activators help an enzyme work rather than slowing it.

questions.q: Polystyrene has the repeating unit –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–, of formula C₈H₈. A chain of 500 such units has a relative molecular mass of (C 12, H 1):
questions.x: C₈H₈ = 8 × 12 + 8 × 1 = 104, and 104 × 500 = 52 000. 48 000 counts only the carbon atoms, and 5200 drops a zero.

questions.q: Polystyrene is an addition polymer of:
questions.x: Styrene (phenylethene) polymerises through its C=C bond to give polystyrene. Chloroethene gives PVC, propene gives polypropene and tetrafluoroethene gives Teflon.

questions.q: A vector of magnitude 10 units has an x-component of 6 units. The magnitude of its y-component is:
questions.x: Magnitude² = x² + y², so y² = 100 − 36 = 64 and y = 8 units. Subtracting 10 − 6 = 4 ignores the right angle between components.

questions.q: The velocity of a body at t = 0, 1, 2 and 3 s is 0, 2, 6 and 12 m s⁻¹. Its acceleration is:
questions.x: The velocity changes by 2, 4 and 6 m s⁻¹ in successive seconds. The changes are unequal and growing, so the acceleration is variable and increasing.

questions.q: For a body moving along a straight line, which quantity can be positive, negative or zero?
questions.x: Displacement has direction, so along a line it can be positive, negative or zero. Distance, speed and time interval can never be negative.

questions.q: Which of the following bodies has a variable acceleration?
o: A stone falling freely in a vacuum
A skydiver falling through air before reaching terminal velocity
A block sliding down a smooth inclined plane
A car moving at a constant velocity
questions.x: As the skydiver speeds up, air resistance grows, so the net force and acceleration keep decreasing. Free fall in a vacuum and a smooth incline give constant acceleration; constant velocity means zero acceleration.

questions.q: Head-on and perfectly elastic: a 2 kg ball at 3 m s⁻¹ strikes a 1 kg ball that is stationary. What are the velocities of the 2 kg and 1 kg balls just after impact?
o: 1 m s⁻¹ and 4 m s⁻¹ forward
2 m s⁻¹ and 2 m s⁻¹ forward
questions.x: Momentum: 2 × 3 = 2v₁ + v₂, so 2v₁ + v₂ = 6. Relative speed: v₂ − v₁ = 3. Solving gives v₁ = 1 m s⁻¹ and v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹, both forward.

questions.q: A body moves back towards the origin: its position is 30 m at t = 0 and 0 m at t = 6 s, changing at a steady rate. What velocity does the slope of its displacement–time graph give?
questions.x: Velocity = slope = (0 − 30) ÷ (6 − 0) = −5 m s⁻¹. The negative sign shows the body is moving back towards the origin.

questions.q: A 3 kg stone is tossed straight up and climbs 4 m before stopping. How much work does gravity do on it during this climb? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.x: Gravity (30 N) acts downward while the stone moves 4 m upward, so θ = 180° and W = 30 × 4 × cos 180° = −120 J.

questions.q: A filament lamp takes in 60 J of electrical energy every second and its efficiency as a light source is 20%. The light energy it gives out each second is:
questions.x: Useful output = 20% of 60 J = 12 J of light; the other 48 J becomes heat. 48 J is the wasted part, not the useful output.

questions.q: A tractor's engine delivers 20 kW while it pulls a trailer with a force of 4000 N in the direction of motion. The speed of the tractor is:
questions.x: P = Fv, so v = 20 000 ÷ 4000 = 5 m s⁻¹. Dividing the force by the power instead gives the wrong 0.2.

questions.q: An angular velocity of 1 rad s⁻¹ is closest to:
questions.x: 1 rad s⁻¹ = 60 rad min⁻¹ = 60/2π ≈ 9.5 rev min⁻¹.

questions.q: A point on a fan blade 0.25 m from the axis travels along an arc of 1.5 m. Through what angle has the blade turned?
questions.x: θ = s/r = 1.5/0.25 = 6 rad. Multiplying the two numbers gives 0.375, which is wrong.

questions.q: Water is carried at high speed through the wide main pipes of a city's water supply. The flow in these pipes is most likely to be:
o: Turbulent, because the speed is high and the pipe is wide
Laminar, because water has low viscosity
Laminar, because the pipe is enclosed
Non-viscous, because the pipe is smooth
questions.x: Large flows at high speed in wide pipes exceed the critical velocity, so, like most practical flows, the flow is turbulent.

questions.q: Pick the everyday flow that is smooth and layered, with no eddies:
o: Smoke billowing from a large fire
Air in the wake behind a jet aircraft
Syrup poured slowly from a spoon in a smooth, unbroken stream
questions.x: Laminar flow occurs at low speeds, especially for viscous liquids such as syrup. The other flows are fast and full of eddies, so they are turbulent.

questions.q: In deriving Bernoulli's equation, the work done by the pressure force at the outlet (narrow) end of the tube is taken as negative because:
o: The pressure there is always negative
The pressure force there acts opposite to the direction in which the fluid moves
The fluid there is at rest
The cross-sectional area there is negative
questions.x: At the outlet, the fluid ahead pushes back on the moving fluid, so the force is opposite to the displacement and the work P₂A₂Δx₂ is negative.

questions.q: When a wave on a string reflects from an end tied to a rigid support, the reflected wave undergoes a phase change of π. As a result, the fixed end of the string is always:
questions.x: The incident and reflected waves are in opposite phase at the fixed end, so their displacements always cancel there. The rigid support cannot move, so it is a node.

questions.q: Aluminium has Young's modulus 7.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa and density 2.8 × 10³ kg m⁻³. The speed of longitudinal sound waves in an aluminium rod is:
questions.x: v = √(E/ρ) = √(7.0 × 10¹⁰ / 2.8 × 10³) = √(2.5 × 10⁷) = 5000 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 2.5 × 10⁷.

questions.q: For any gas, the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is:
o: Greater than 1, because Cp is always larger than Cv
Less than 1, because Cv is larger than Cp
questions.x: At constant pressure some of the heat supplied also does work as the gas expands, so Cp > Cv and γ > 1. That is why Laplace's speed √(γP/ρ) is larger than Newton's √(P/ρ).

questions.q: A pipe open at both ends sounds its fundamental note, of wavelength 1.6 m. Neglecting end correction, the length of the pipe is:
questions.x: For an open pipe the fundamental has λ = 2L, so L = 1.6/2 = 0.8 m. 0.4 m would apply to a closed pipe (λ = 4L).

questions.q: For longitudinal sound waves along a thin solid rod, the modulus E in v = √(E/ρ) is:
o: The bulk modulus of the surrounding air
The shear modulus of the material
The pressure of the surrounding air
questions.x: In a thin rod the material is stretched and compressed along its length, so Young's modulus applies. For a gas or liquid the bulk modulus is used instead.

questions.q: A simple flute is modelled as a tube 0.85 m long, open at both ends. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹ and ignoring end effects, its first overtone has a frequency of:
questions.x: Fundamental f₁ = v/2L = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz. An open tube gives all harmonics, so the first overtone is 2 × 200 = 400 Hz; 600 Hz would be the next one after that.

questions.q: The temperature of a cup of tea falls from 80 °C to 50 °C. The fall in temperature on the kelvin scale is:
questions.x: One kelvin and one degree Celsius are the same size step, so a temperature difference of 30 °C is also 30 K. Only actual temperatures differ by 273.

questions.q: A student records the heat needed per mole per kelvin for a gas. The SI unit she should write is:
questions.x: Molar specific heat is heat per mole per kelvin, so its unit is J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the unit of specific heat, and J K⁻¹ is that of heat capacity.

questions.q: A gas does 500 J of work while expanding at a constant pressure of 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa. The increase in its volume is:
questions.x: W = PΔV, so ΔV = 500 ÷ (2.5 × 10⁵) = 2 × 10⁻³ m³. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 1.25 × 10⁸.

questions.q: The electric potential at a distance r from a point charge is V. At a distance r/3 from the same charge, the potential is:
questions.x: V ∝ 1/r, so making the distance one third makes the potential three times as large. Nine times would apply to the field.

questions.q: For a very large plate carrying positive charge, the electric field on its two sides is:
o: Pointing towards the plate on both sides
Perpendicular to the plate and pointing away from it on both sides
Pointing away on one side and towards it on the other
Parallel to the plate on both sides
questions.x: A positive plate repels a positive test charge on either side, so the field lines leave the plate perpendicularly on both faces.

questions.q: In deriving V = kq/r, the work done in bringing a test charge from infinity is found by adding up the work over many small steps. This is necessary because:
o: The test charge changes during the motion
The electric force is zero at every point
The electric force on the test charge changes with distance
questions.x: Coulomb's force varies as 1/r², so it is not constant over the path. The work is found by summing (integrating) F Δr over small steps where F is nearly constant.

questions.q: A source with internal resistance 4 Ω delivers its greatest possible power, 9 W, to a matched load. The emf of the source is:
questions.x: Maximum power = E²/4r, so E² = 4 × 4 × 9 = 144 and E = 12 V. Using E²/r gives 6 V.

questions.q: Three lamps are connected in series to a battery, and a steady current flows. The current is:
o: Largest in the lamp nearest the positive terminal
The same at every point of the circuit
Smallest in the last lamp, because it is used up
questions.x: In a steady current charge is not used up or stored anywhere, so the same charge passes every cross-section of a series circuit per second.

questions.q: A particle of charge q moves in a circle of radius r at right angles to a uniform field B. The magnitude of its momentum is:
questions.x: From r = mv/(qB), the momentum mv = qBr.

questions.q: Making the iron core of a transformer from thin insulated laminations mainly reduces the energy lost through:
o: Leakage of flux out of the core
questions.x: Insulated laminations break up the paths of eddy currents in the core. Winding heating is reduced by thick wire and hysteresis by using soft iron.

questions.q: In a pure inductor, the current lags behind the applied voltage because:
o: The self-induced back emf opposes every change in the current
The inductor stores charge on its turns
The inductor's resistance rises with current
The magnetic field leaks out of the coil
questions.x: Any change in current induces a back emf that opposes it, so the current builds up a quarter-cycle after the voltage.

questions.q: A forward-biased silicon diode (drop 0.7 V) is in series with a resistor R across a 3.7 V battery. The current is 6 mA. What is R?
questions.x: Voltage across R = 3.7 − 0.7 = 3.0 V, so R = 3.0/0.006 = 500 Ω. Ignoring the diode drop gives 617 Ω.

questions.q: The intensity of a beam of monochromatic light is doubled while its frequency is kept the same. What happens to the photons?
o: Each photon has the same energy, but twice as many arrive per second
Each photon has twice the energy, with the same number per second
Each photon has half the energy, with four times as many per second
Each photon moves at twice the speed
questions.x: Photon energy depends only on frequency (E = hf). A brighter beam simply carries more photons per second.

questions.q: White light passes through cool hydrogen gas at room temperature. The absorption lines seen belong almost entirely to the Lyman series because:
o: Lyman lines are the only lines in the visible region
Only electrons in n = 2 can absorb light
Cool atoms can only emit, not absorb, photons
Nearly all the atoms are in the ground state, n = 1
questions.x: At room temperature almost every hydrogen atom is in n = 1, so absorption starts from that level, giving Lyman lines (in the ultraviolet).

questions.q: People who work with radioactive sources wear a film badge or dosimeter in order to:
o: Shield their bodies from gamma rays
Stop alpha particles from reaching their skin
Make the sources decay more quickly
Record the radiation dose they have received
questions.x: A badge or dosimeter monitors exposure so that a worker's dose can be kept within safe limits. It gives no real shielding.

questions.q: Technetium-99m is widely used as a medical tracer mainly because it:
o: Emits alpha particles that are easy to detect outside the body
Has a half-life of thousands of years
Is not radioactive once inside the body
Emits only gamma rays and has a half-life of about 6 hours
questions.x: Its gamma rays escape the body to reach a detector, while its short half-life (about 6 h) keeps the patient's dose low. Alpha particles would not leave the body.

questions.q: Many people believe that a camel stores water in its hump, but the hump is really a store of fat. When food is short, the camel uses this fat for energy, and the hump becomes smaller and may even flop to one side. A camel can lose a quarter of its body weight in water and still survive, and when it finds water it can drink more than a hundred litres in a few minutes. Which statement is supported by the passage?
o: A camel's hump stores water for long journeys
A camel's hump gets smaller when the camel uses its stored fat
A camel dies if it loses a quarter of its body weight in water
A camel needs several hours to drink a hundred litres
questions.x: The passage says the camel uses the fat in its hump when food is short, and the hump becomes smaller. It states the hump holds fat, not water, and that the camel survives losing a quarter of its weight in water.

questions.q: Pick the sentence in which the linking phrase is used without error.
o: Despite of the fog, the flight left on time.
Although of the fog, the flight left on time.
In spite the fog, the flight left on time.
In spite of the fog, the flight left on time.
questions.x: 'In spite of' and 'despite' (without 'of') are followed by a noun; 'despite of' and 'although of' are not English.

questions.q: In which sentence is the apostrophe used correctly with a plural noun?
o: The childrens' toys were scattered everywhere.
The childrens toys were scattered everywhere.
The children's toys were scattered everywhere.
The children's' toys were scattered everywhere.
questions.x: 'Children' is a plural not ending in s, so it takes apostrophe + s: children's.

questions.q: Which sentence contains an error in word order after a negative adverb?
o: Seldom do we go to the cinema these days.
Never before had the town seen such a flood.
Seldom we go to the cinema these days.
Little did Sara know what was coming.
questions.x: After 'Seldom' at the start, inversion is needed ('Seldom do we go'); the other three invert correctly.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "___ you work regularly, you will not do well in the test."
questions.x: 'Unless' means 'if not': if you do not work regularly, you will not do well.

questions.q: Change into the passive voice: "They made Bilal captain of the team."
o: Captain was made Bilal of the team.
Bilal was made captain of the team.
Bilal is made captain of the team.
Bilal was making captain of the team.
questions.x: With 'make + object + complement', the object 'Bilal' becomes the subject and the complement 'captain' stays after the verb.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "Ali loves cricket, ___ his brother prefers hockey."
questions.x: 'Whereas' joins two contrasting facts about two people.

questions.q: Which sentence makes it clear that Ali, not Bilal, was ill?
o: Ali told Bilal that he was ill.
Bilal was told by Ali that he was ill.
Ali and Bilal said that he was ill.
questions.x: In direct speech 'I' can only mean the speaker, Ali. In the other sentences 'he' could refer to either boy, so the meaning is unclear.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "The girl who sings in the choir and plays the sitar ____ my cousin."
questions.x: The main subject is 'the girl'; 'who sings ... and plays the sitar' describes her. A singular subject takes 'is'.

questions.q: Which evidence gives the strongest support for the belief that seat belts reduce injuries in car crashes?
o: In crashes at similar speeds, belted passengers had fewer serious injuries than unbelted ones
Most new cars are sold with seat belts already fitted
A well-known driver always wears his seat belt
Many people find seat belts uncomfortable on long journeys
questions.x: Comparing belted and unbelted people in similar crashes tests the belief directly. That cars have belts, or a famous person uses one, says nothing about injuries.

questions.q: Which number is wrong in the series 2, 5, 8, 12, 14, 17?
questions.x: The series should go up by 3 each time: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17. So 12 should be 11.

questions.q: Find the missing number: 100, 91, ?, 73, 64
questions.x: Each term is 9 less than the one before: 91 - 9 = 82, and 82 - 9 = 73 checks.

questions.q: Four books, red, green, blue and yellow, stand in a row on a shelf. The red book is at the left end. The green book is immediately to the right of the red book. The blue book is not at the right end. Which book is at the right end?
questions.x: Red and green take the first two places. Blue cannot be last, so blue is third and yellow is at the right end.

questions.q: Five students got different marks in a test. Sana got more than Zain but less than Omar. Hira got less than Zain. Kinza got more than Omar. Who got the second lowest marks?
questions.x: From highest: Kinza, Omar, Sana, Zain, Hira. Hira is lowest, so Zain is second lowest.

questions.q: Statement: Doctors in a city link a rise in eye and skin infections to public swimming pools whose water is not properly treated. Courses of action: I. The pools' water should be tested and kept properly chlorinated. II. Swimming should be banned in the city forever. III. All public swimming pools in the city should be demolished. Which course(s) of action follow?
o: I, II and III all follow
questions.x: Testing and treating the water removes the cause of the infections. A permanent ban on swimming and demolishing every pool are extreme steps that go far beyond fixing the problem.

questions.q: Statement: Floods damaged the only bridge of a town, cutting off villages on the far side from the town's hospital. Courses of action: I. The bridge should be repaired or a temporary crossing built as soon as possible. II. Emergency medical help, such as a mobile clinic or boat service, should be arranged for the cut-off villages meanwhile. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Action I restores the link, which takes time. Action II meets the urgent medical need until then. They work together, so both follow.

questions.q: A car would not start on a cold morning. Its headlights did not come on and its horn made no sound. What is the most likely cause?
o: One of the tyres was flat
questions.x: The starter, lights and horn all run on the battery, so one flat battery explains all three. An empty fuel tank would not stop the lights or horn working.

questions.q: Some people believe that a black cat crossing the road brings bad luck. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: A cat's path has no possible link to later events, and there is no evidence of such an effect
Many people in the town believe it
Black cats are rarer than other cats
Cats cross roads mostly at night
questions.x: A belief needs a link between cause and effect and evidence to support it. Popularity or how often cats cross roads proves nothing.
